channel_meaning: Bearing 3, channel 1 of its pair (per IMS README: Bearing 3 = Ch5&6, 1-indexed; channel=4 here is 0-indexed = Ch5)
documented_failure: IMS vendor README states only: 'At the end of the test-to-failure experiment, inner race defect occurred in bearing 3 and roller element defect in bearing 4.' No per-file label, no severity scale, no timestamp of onset is provided by the dataset.

option_a_binary_normal_degraded.description: healthy vs degraded, single z-score threshold on RMS relative to an early baseline
option_a_binary_normal_degraded.defensibility: High - a single, sharp, well-evidenced step-change exists at file ~156 (RMS z-score jumps from ~2 to ~38 within a handful of files). Simple, reproducible.
option_a_binary_normal_degraded.limitation: Loses the distinction between 'developing fault, keep monitoring' and 'severe, act now' - the single most operationally useful distinction for predictive maintenance.
option_a_binary_normal_degraded.verdict: Defensible, but discards real information the data actually supports.

option_b_three_class_healthy_degrading_s.description: healthy / degrading / severe, using two independent z-scored signals (RMS for the healthy cutoff, kurtosis for the severe cutoff)
option_b_three_class_healthy_degrading_s.defensibility: High, but only after rejecting a naive single-signal version - see 'rejected_naive_rule' below. The final rule is grounded in a real, observed physical distinction: RMS saturates almost immediately after fault onset and stops discriminating severity, while kurtosis (impulsiveness) stays near-baseline through the elevated-but-stable plateau and only escalates sharply and increasingly frequently from file ~1900 onward (z-scores of 39, 117, 161 observed vs. a near-baseline 0-8 range for most of the preceding 1700 files) - consistent with the textbook progression of rolling-element bearing spalling (energy rise first, then increasing impulsive impacts as spalling worsens).
option_b_three_class_healthy_degrading_s.limitation: The 'severe' label is not a clean monotonic tail - it appears as increasingly frequent intermittent bursts from ~30% through the timeline onward, interleaved with 'degrading' labels, before becoming dominant near the end. This is treated as a real physical characteristic (intermittent impact events before continuous severe degradation), not label noise - but it does mean per-file classification near these transitions is a genuinely harder problem than a single clean boundary.
option_b_three_class_healthy_degrading_s.verdict: Selected. Richer, operationally more useful, and defensible from the data's own two-signal structure - not from an arbitrary composite score.

option_c_continuous_health_index_regress.description: 0-100 index, a deterministic rescaling of max(z_rms, z_kurtosis)
option_c_continuous_health_index_regress.defensibility: Mathematically valid (same underlying evidence as option B, just not discretized), but MAE/RMSE/R2 against this target only measures how well a model recovers a SELF-CONSISTENT DERIVED INDEX from engineered features - it is not evaluable against any independent ground-truth health measurement, because none exists in this dataset.
option_c_continuous_health_index_regress.limitation: Highest risk of being misread as 'the model predicts true machine health' when it actually predicts 'the model predicts the same statistical rule used to label it, from correlated features'.
option_c_continuous_health_index_regress.verdict: Computed and included in the manifest (health_index field) for future use, but NOT selected as the primary baseline-model target this task - would require its own dedicated framing to avoid the interpretation risk above.

rejected_naive_rule.description: First attempt: severity_z = max(z_rms, z_kurtosis), thresholded at 3/10 (reusing this codebase's existing anomaly_z_threshold and fusion severity_z_cap directly).
rejected_naive_rule.why_rejected: Produced a degenerate distribution when checked against the FULL 2156-file trajectory (not assumed from prior sparse sampling, per this task's instruction): 2000/2156 files (93%) labelled 'severe', 'degrading' left with only 3 single-file transient blips. Root cause: RMS alone drives severity_z past 10 almost immediately after onset and never comes back down, because the healthy baseline's RMS std (0.00074) is extremely tight - any real post-onset RMS value produces an enormous z-score regardless of how far along the actual degradation trajectory really is.
rejected_naive_rule.lesson: This is the same finding as the earlier IDEA LAB demo-baseline investigation (Phase 7 / the 19-hour-audit fix task): z-scores against an extremely tight baseline saturate almost immediately and stop being informative for GRADUATED severity, even though they remain excellent for a binary healthy/not-healthy signal.

label_construction_rule.statement: THE IMS DATASET PROVIDES NO PER-FILE GROUND-TRUTH LABEL OF ANY KIND. Every label below is DERIVED by applying a documented statistical rule to the dataset's own engineered features. It must never be described or logged as original dataset ground truth.
label_construction_rule.baseline_period: files [0, 100) - independently re-verified flat/stable in this task's full-trajectory scan (RMS mean=0.1311, std=0.00074; kurtosis mean=3.379, std=0.093)
label_construction_rule.rule: z_rms and z_kurtosis computed against that baseline for every file. healthy: z_rms < 3.0. severe: z_kurtosis >= 10.0 (checked independently of z_rms). degrading: everything else (i.e. z_rms >= 3.0 and z_kurtosis < 10.0).
label_construction_rule.thresholds_source: 3.0 matches app.core.config.settings.anomaly_z_threshold; 10.0 matches app.fusion.engine.FusionEngine's severity_z_cap - reused for internal consistency with the rest of IDEA LAB, not tuned to this specific file range.

split_strategy.description: Chronological-within-stratum block split (NOT a pure global chronological cut).
split_strategy.why_pure_chronological_split_was_rejecte: A global 70/15/15 chronological cut was computed and checked before deciding: it placed only 20/323 (6%) severe files in train and 264/323 (82%) in test - severe files are naturally back-loaded in time (real degradation worsens near end-of-life), so a naive global cut would starve training of the rarest, operationally most important class.
split_strategy.method: The 2156-file timeline is split into contiguous 20-file blocks (temporal adjacency preserved - no shuffling). Each block is assigned a 'dominant label' (majority vote among its files) purely to decide its stratum; individual files keep their own true derived label regardless. Within each dominant-label stratum, blocks are sorted chronologically and split 70/15/15 (earliest -> train, middle -> validation, latest -> test).
split_strategy.residual_leakage_risk: Adjacent files immediately across a stratum-internal block boundary (e.g. the last file of a train-assigned block next to the first file of a validation-assigned block from the same stratum) are temporally close and could be mildly correlated - this is a documented, accepted residual risk analogous to the boundary risk in the thermal dataset split (see docs/THERMAL_SPLIT_REPORT.md), not eliminated here given the added complexity of block-level buffering on top of stratification. It affects a small fraction of files at stratum boundaries, not the bulk of the split.

feature_set_note: Drawn entirely from the existing, already-validated app.pipelines.vibration.features.extract_vibration_features output - no new feature engineering, no raw-waveform deep model in this baseline task.
unit_of_analysis: One IMS file (20,480 samples = 1.024s snapshot at 20kHz) = one sample/observation, matching how the existing demo pipeline already treats these files as natural analysis windows. No sub-windowing was introduced.
